items.prose: A fund's monthly returns have mean 1.2% and sd 4%.
items.question: What is its annualised Sharpe ratio? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Monthly ratio times $\sqrt{12}$.

byKey.x12: You multiplied by 12. The sd grows with $\sqrt{12}$, so the ratio does too.
byKey.x252: You used the daily factor on monthly data.

explain.text: $1.2/4 = 0.3$ a month; twelve months a year gives $0.3 \times 3.46 = 1.04$.

items.question: What is the maximum drawdown, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each fall from the highest value before it.

byKey.first: That is the first fall, from £130k. A deeper one comes later.
byKey.range: You compared the last value with the first high. Use the running peak, £140k.
byKey.pos: Right size; the course writes drawdowns as negative.

explain.text: The running peak reaches £140k before the fall to £98k: $98/140 - 1 = -0.30$. The fall from £130k to £117k is only −10%.

items.prose: A rule has a gross Sharpe ratio of 1.2 and volatility of 12% a year. Its turnover is 0.5 a day and each unit traded costs 5 bp.
items.question: What is its net Sharpe ratio? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Yearly drag over yearly volatility is the fall in Sharpe.

byKey.flip: You halved the turnover. 0.5 is already the two-sided figure.
byKey.daily: You took one day's cost off. Drag is a yearly number: multiply by 252.

explain.text: The drag is $0.5 \times 252 \times 0.0005 = 6.3\%$ a year. Dividing by the 12% volatility gives 0.525 off the Sharpe: $1.2 - 0.525 = 0.675$.

items.prose: Daily means: strategy 0.05%, buy and hold 0.04%. The strategy's beta is 0.8.
items.question: What is its annual alpha, in %? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mean minus beta times the benchmark's mean, times 252.

byKey.excess: That subtracts the whole benchmark mean. Subtract 0.8 times it.
byKey.daily: That is alpha per day. Multiply by 252.

explain.text: $0.05 - 0.8 \times 0.04 = 0.018\%$ a day of return beta does not explain, times 252 is 4.5% a year.

items.prose: Two strategies have exactly the same daily returns over a year, in a different order. In B the losing days come in one long run.
items.question: Which is true?

options.text: Same Sharpe ratio, B has the deeper maximum drawdown.
B has the lower Sharpe ratio, because its losses cluster.
options.why: The Sharpe uses only the mean and sd of the returns, which the order does not change.

options.text: Same Sharpe and same drawdown, since the returns are the same.
options.why: Drawdown depends on the path. A run of losses compounds into one deep fall.

options.text: B ends lower, because losses compound.
options.why: Multiplication does not care about order: the final value is the same.

feedback.correct: Order changes drawdown, not Sharpe or the final value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which numbers depend on the order of returns?

explain.text: The mean, the sd and the product of $(1 + r)$ ignore order. The running peak does not: a run of losses compounds from one high, so B's maximum drawdown is deeper.

items.prose: A backtest on three years of daily data shows an annualised Sharpe ratio of 0.9. Use Lo's standard error.
items.question: What is the standard error? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With daily data the error is about $1/\sqrt{\text{years}}$.

byKey.yearly: You treated the data as three yearly returns. They are 756 daily ones.
byKey.days: That is the per-day error. Annualise it: multiply by $\sqrt{252}$.

explain.text: The daily Sharpe is $0.9/\sqrt{252} = 0.057$, so $SE = \sqrt{(1 + 0.057^2/2)/756} \times \sqrt{252} = 0.58$. Three years leave 0.9 short of two errors from zero.

items.prose: A strategy turns £1m into £1.5m over four years of daily data (1,008 returns). Its maximum drawdown is −25%.
items.question: What is its Calmar ratio? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compound the growth to a yearly rate first.

byKey.simple: You divided 50% by 4 years. Growth compounds: $1.5^{1/4} - 1 = 10.7\%$.
byKey.total: You used the total 50% return. Calmar uses the yearly rate.

items.prose: A report plots a daily-trading strategy's **gross** equity against buy and hold, and says it beat the market by 6% a year. Its turnover is 1.2 a day; costs are 2.5 bp per unit traded.
items.question: What should the reviewer say?

options.text: Compare net with net: costs of about 7.6% a year erase the 6% lead.
Fair enough: buy and hold is shown gross too.
options.why: Buy and hold trades once; the strategy trades 1.2 of the book every day. Gross against gross hides that difference.

options.text: Costs of 2.5 bp are too small to matter.
options.why: Small per trade, large per year: $1.2 \times 252 \times 2.5$ bp is 7.6%.

options.text: Add the costs to buy and hold instead.
options.why: Buy and hold pays one entry cost. The strategy must pay its own.

feedback.correct: Net against net, and the lead disappears.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the strategy's yearly cost drag.

explain.text: The drag is $1.2 \times 252 \times 0.00025 = 7.6\%$ a year, more than the 6% lead. Comparing gross with gross flatters whichever side trades more.

items.prose: A rule held a position on 180 days of a 252-day year and made money on 99 of them. It was flat on the other 72 days.
items.question: What is its hit rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Hits over days with a position.

byKey.all: You divided by all 252 days. Flat days are left out.
byKey.flat-hits: You counted flat days as hits.

explain.text: $99/180 = 0.55$. Flat days are neither hits nor misses, so they leave the count.
